strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper articulates two concrete limitations of centralized routing (inflexibility of retraining and inaccurate capability assessment by small routers) and offers a coherent paradigm shift toward distributed self-routing.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 5-agent homogeneous cascade with 8 diverse baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, AutoMix, FORC, GraphRouter, plus naive baselines) across three cost-preference scenarios, with additional out-of-domain generalization (Tables 3, 13, 14) and reduced-agent modularity experiments (Tables 4, 15, 16).

Thoughtful analysis section: the easy/hard query cost analysis (Figure 6), the intrinsic-vs-external classifier comparison (Table 5), the answer/reject accuracy split (Figure 7), and the ΔPerformance analysis (Figure 8, Appendix J) all directly support the core claims rather than only reporting aggregate numbers.

The scenario-conditioned reward with the reliability factor γ is a clean mechanism that empirically achieves system-level scenario adaptation (Figures 4, 5) from a single trained system, unlike baselines requiring per-scenario retraining.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed training hyperparameters, prompts, data construction templates, and per-dataset model performance/cost tables in the appendices; routing overhead is empirically quantified (Appendix A, Table 6) rather than simply asserted.
The paper is honest about caveats: it validates that training does not materially improve task capability (<1% ΔPerformance), and confines modularity claims to what is actually tested.
weaknesses: The 'distributed' framing is stronger than what is demonstrated: only a strictly ordered cascade with single-direction routing (Eq. 4) is evaluated, which is functionally close to FrugalGPT-style cascading with self-assessment. Tree/mesh topologies—the actual distinguishing feature of a distributed network—are deferred entirely to future work, so the novelty over cascade-with-rejection methods is narrower than claimed.

Limited technical novelty in the training pipeline: the SFT stage closely follows prior rejection/reliability work (Xu et al., 2024), and the RL reward is a simple correctness/rejection trade-off. The reward rationality analysis (Eqs. 8-10) is a straightforward expected-value threshold argument rather than a substantive theoretical contribution.

Some baseline comparisons raise fairness concerns: RouteLLM's reported accuracy (0.44) is below even the smallest-model baseline and appears under-tuned relative to published results; baselines were modified (e.g., substituting DistilBERT score models with Qwen2.5-0.5B) in ways whose sensitivity is not analyzed. DiSRouter also fine-tunes all pool LLMs while routers do not; the <1% ΔPerformance check partially mitigates but does not fully eliminate this asymmetry.

Inconsistent results in some settings: on OOD data under the Cost First scenario, the SFT variant underperforms several baselines (utility 0.25 vs. FrugalGPT 0.38), and overall gains shrink as α increases; the dependence on the RL stage for the main claims in this regime deserves more discussion. No variance estimates, error bars, or significance tests are reported.

Homogeneous model pool (all Qwen2.5 sizes) and only QA-style benchmarks with in-domain training drawn from the same seven datasets used for evaluation limit external validity; behavior with heterogeneous model families, stronger frontier models, or generative open-ended tasks is untested.

Cost modeling is simplified: fixed normalized costs independent of query, latency-based cost used inconsistently with abstract cost values, and reward optimality is analyzed per-agent without accounting for cascade-level effects (e.g., downstream routing uncertainty of later agents).

strengths: The problem formulation is clear and well-structured, with a clean decomposition of routing into centralized vs. distributed policies and a formal utility objective

The evaluation is fairly comprehensive for the chosen setting: comparisons against eight baselines across three preference scenarios, out-of-domain generalization tests, a reduced-agent modularity study, a direct intrinsic-vs-external classifier comparison (Table 5), and a sanity check that training does not inflate task performance (Appendix J)

The scenario-adaptability mechanism (preference factor α injected via prompts and reward) is a practical feature, and the system/agent-level routing distribution analyses (Figures 4–5) provide concrete evidence that agents adjust their answer thresholds coherently
Implementation details (training hyperparameters, data construction, prompts) are documented sufficiently to support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core mechanism is a confidence/rejection-based cascade of LLMs, which is very close to FrugalGPT-style cascading combined with 'I don't know' rejection training (the SFT data construction is explicitly adopted from Xu et al., 2024) and AutoMix's self-assessment routing. The 'distributed self-routing' framing adds a new name more than a new mechanism

The 'distributed' claims are largely untested: all experiments use a strict linear cascade with a fixed entry point, one-directional routing, and a mandatory fallback agent. Tree/mesh topologies and true inter-agent routing are relegated to future work, so the headline generality of the paradigm is not demonstrated

Restricted model pool: only five homogeneous Qwen2.5-Instruct models (0.5B–14B) are used. Claims about self-awareness generalizing across agents, plug-and-play modularity, and flexibility to add arbitrary new LLMs are unverified for heterogeneous families, black-box API models, or fine-tuned specialists

The central claim that intrinsic self-assessment beats external assessment (Table 5) has confounds: ground-truth labels are generated from the same model's greedy responses, both the intrinsic and external classifiers are trained on the same 10k samples, and only one model size (7B) is tested; a stronger external router trained on more data could change the conclusion

Several reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence: Table 1 costs/performance do not match Appendix Table 10 averages; Automix is reported with cost 1.10 despite a defined cost range [0,1]; the SFT variant achieves higher accuracy than the RL variant in the Performance First scenario, which is never adequately explained

Utility improvements are driven substantially by reduced accuracy (e.g., RL lowers accuracy from 0.84 to 0.81 in Performance First, 0.83 to 0.77 in Balance, 0.69 to 0.67 OOD); no analysis is given of error/abstention trade-offs or user-facing consequences of the accuracy degradation
No statistical significance testing, variance reporting, or multiple runs; differences between DiSRouter and the strongest baselines (e.g., GraphRouter) are moderate and could be within noise

The reward design assumes routing costs are negligible, but the analysis in Appendix A is only timing-based and specific to their setup; cost modeling for cascading rejection responses in latency-sensitive deployments deserves more care

strengths: Clear and well-motivated paradigm shift from centralized routing to distributed self-routing, with a precise problem formulation (Section 2) that cleanly separates centralized vs. distributed policies.

The localized, scenario-conditioned reward (Eq. 7) is an elegant design: it enables fully independent, parallel training of agents while still achieving system-level adaptability to the preference factor alpha, supported by the reward rationality analysis (Eqs. 8-10, Figure 3).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 8 baselines including strong recent routers (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, Automix, FORC, GraphRouter), 3 cost scenarios, in-domain and out-of-domain generalization (Tables 2-3), and a plug-and-play modularity test with a reduced 3-agent system (Table 4).

Good mechanistic analysis of why the method works: system-level routing distributions (Figure 4), agent-level answer rates (Figure 5), easy/hard query cost discrimination (Figure 6), and a direct external-vs-intrinsic classifier comparison (Table 5) that substantiates the core claim.

Careful fairness checks: Appendix J quantifies that task capability barely changes (<1%) after self-awareness training, addressing the concern that gains come from improved task performance rather than routing; Appendix A empirically justifies the negligible routing-overhead assumption.
The scenario adaptability result (a single trained system adjusting behavior via prompts, unlike scenario-dependent baselines) is a practical and non-trivial advantage.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: all agents are from a single model family (Qwen2.5-Instruct, 0.5B-14B). Heterogeneous pools (different families, different providers) are not tested, which weakens the claims of generality and real-world applicability of the 'distributed' paradigm.

Despite the 'distributed network' framing, the actual instantiation and all experiments are restricted to a simple linear cascade, which is architecturally close to existing cascade methods (FrugalGPT-style escalation with per-model rejection). Tree/mesh topologies are only discussed in Section 6, so the claimed flexibility/scalability advantages over cascades remain largely unvalidated.

Novelty is somewhat incremental: the SFT stage builds directly on prior rejection/reliability training (Xu et al., 2024) and the RL reward is a simple threshold-style rule; the main contribution is the combination and the localized reward design rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The 'plug-and-play' claim is partially overstated: while removing agents requires no retraining, adding a new agent still requires the full Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT+RL) for that agent, plus its own capability-estimation data. This is not experimentally demonstrated (only agent removal, not addition, is tested).

Some baseline results appear suspiciously weak (e.g., RouteLLM at 0.44 accuracy, below the Random baseline), raising concerns about baseline tuning even though implementation details are provided; without variance estimates or significance tests, the utility gaps in Tables 2-4 are hard to assess statistically.

Utility metric sensitivity: the SFT vs. SFT+RL comparison shows meaningful accuracy drops (e.g., 0.84->0.81 Performance First; 0.83->0.77 Balance) traded for cost; the paper does not analyze when a user would prefer the SFT-only system, and accuracy loss in Cost First OOD (SFT 0.69 vs RL 0.67) complicates the 'consistently better' narrative.

All in-domain training data is drawn from the same datasets used for in-domain evaluation, and cost is a fixed normalized constant rather than measured inference cost in the utility computation (measured latencies are only in Appendix E), which slightly weakens the realism of the cost-utility claims.
Minor writing issues (e.g., 'To further enhancing self-awareness', 'has also been proven to be more effective') and occasional overclaiming ('prove') that should be tempered.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper identifies two concrete limitations of centralized routers (fixed LLM pool, weak capability assessment) and proposes a coherent distributed alternative where routing is realized via learned rejection behavior.

The Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT + scenario-conditioned RL with a localized reward) is well designed, and the reward rationality analysis (Eqs. 8-10, Figure 3) provides a principled justification for the (1-alpha)^gamma rejection reward.

Comprehensive and multi-dimensional evaluation: in-domain and out-of-domain generalization, heterogeneous model families (Gemma-3, Phi-4), closed-source GPT-series experiments with no training, open-ended generative tasks with adapted rewards, plug-and-play 3-agent ablation, latency/overhead analysis, and a Delta-Pass@10 control showing gains are not from improved task capability.

Strong analysis sections: system-level routing distributions (Figure 4), agent-level answer rates (Figure 5), easy/hard query cost separation (Figure 6), and the external-classifier vs. intrinsic self-assessment comparison (Table 5) directly support the central claim.
Reproducibility is well supported: datasets, model pool, training hyperparameters, baseline implementations, and prompts/templates are all documented in detail.
weaknesses: Limited novelty in the core mechanism: the method is essentially a cost-ordered cascade with abstention training ('I don't know'), which combines well-known ideas from FrugalGPT cascades, rejection/reliability fine-tuning (Xu et al., 2024), and self-verification routing (AutoMix). The 'distributed paradigm' framing is somewhat inflated, since the evaluated topology is a fixed cascade where each agent can only route forward, so routing decisions are binary reject-or-answer rather than genuinely flexible distributed routing.

The localized reward ignores inter-agent dependencies: an agent's optimal rejection threshold should depend on downstream agents' capabilities, but each agent is trained independently using only its own correctness probability. The paper does not theoretically or empirically analyze when this decomposition is suboptimal, nor how much utility is lost relative to a jointly optimized cascade.

Utility gains over the strongest baseline (GraphRouter) are meaningful but not dramatic (e.g., 0.73 vs 0.68 in Performance First), and no statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple-run variance are reported, making it hard to judge robustness of the improvements.

The main experiments use a homogeneous Qwen2.5 family with fixed normalized per-model costs; the headline results depend on this cost assignment, and token-based or pricing-based cost modeling is only touched on in appendix experiments.

The central claim that 'intrinsic self-assessment is more effective than external assessment' rests mainly on one binary-classification experiment (Table 5); the confound of model scale is only partially controlled (7B internal vs. 8B external), and the external classifiers may be under-tuned relative to the extensively trained DiSRouter agents.
No code or data release is stated, which limits reproducibility despite the detailed description, and the discussion of alternative topologies (tree/mesh) remains purely speculative.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation: multiple baselines (RouteLLM, FrugalGPT, Automix, FORC, GraphRouter), three cost-preference scenarios, out-of-domain datasets, reduced-agent modularity tests, and latency/overhead analysis in the appendix.

Useful supporting analyses, including verification that training does not inflate task capability (ΔPass@10 in A.8), evaluation of intrinsic self-awareness of open-source vs. closed-source LLMs (A.9), heterogeneous model families (A.10), and an extension to open-ended generative tasks (A.11).

The scenario-conditioned reward with the reliability factor γ is a reasonable mechanism for aligning abstention thresholds with user cost/accuracy preferences, and the reward rationality analysis (Eq. 8–10) gives the design some principled grounding.
The paper is generally clearly written, with the routing procedure, training pipeline, and evaluation protocol described in enough detail to understand the method.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core method is essentially a model cascade (FrugalGPT-style, ordered by cost) where each LLM has been aligned to abstain ('I don't know') instead of using an external verifier. Rejection/abstention training exists (Xu et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025), cascades with per-stage confidence are well studied, and the paper itself cites AgentNet (Yang et al., 2025) as decentralized routing. The main delta—mixing three scenario conditions into SFT/RL data and a scenario-conditioned reward—is incremental.

Overclaimed framing relative to the evidence: the paper is sold as 'distributed routing' with superior scalability and generality, but all main experiments use a simple linear cascade; tree/mesh topologies are only discussed as future work. The empirical claims do not substantiate the 'distributed paradigm' contribution.

Potential unfairness in baseline implementation: the score models of FrugalGPT and FORC were replaced with Qwen2.5-0.5B because the original DistilBERT 'performed poorly in our initial trials,' and RouteLLM's accuracy (0.44) barely exceeds always-routing-to-smallest (0.38), raising the possibility that centralized baselines were under-tuned. Some conclusions of superiority may not be robust.

The key 'intrinsic self-assessment beats external assessment' claim (Table 5) rests on a narrow experiment: a single target model (7B), a single task formulation, and balanced binary sampling; it does not establish the general claim made in the abstract and conclusion.

Cost model is artificial: fixed normalized costs (0.1–0.9) in the main experiments rather than real API pricing or measured compute, and routing overhead (>5% in worst case, admitted in A.1) is excluded from the utility metric, which slightly favors the method.

The 'self-awareness' terminology overstates what is being measured; the models are trained to output a fixed rejection string, which is closer to calibrated abstention than intrinsic self-knowledge. Results in A.9.1 showing near-random rejection behavior in base models partly undermine the intrinsic-awareness narrative.
Utility results depend on the arbitrary choice of α values and the γ hyperparameter; sensitivity of results to γ (fixed at 0.5 without ablation) and to the SFT rejection threshold δ is not analyzed.
No code or data release is indicated, weakening reproducibility despite the reproducibility statement.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and well-motivated paradigm shift from centralized routers to distributed, self-routing agents, addressing genuine limitations of existing routing systems (inflexibility to agent-pool changes, inaccurate capability assessment by small external routers).

The proposed two-stage Self-Awareness Training pipeline (SFT for rejection behavior + scenario-conditioned RL) is technically coherent, and the reward rationality analysis (Eqs. 7-10, Figure 3) provides a principled justification for the threshold induced by the preference factor α and reliability factor γ.

Evaluation is unusually comprehensive: three cost scenarios, in-domain and out-of-domain generalization, heterogeneous model families (Gemma, Phi-4, GPT series), plug-and-play modularity tests (3-agent reduction without retraining), open-ended generative tasks with continuous rewards, latency analysis, and a fairness check (Appendix A.8, ΔPass@10) showing gains stem from routing rather than improved task capability.

Insightful analysis sections: the external-router vs. intrinsic self-assessment comparison (Table 5), the easy/hard query cost analysis (Figure 6), and the answered vs. rejected accuracy analysis (Figure 7) directly support the central claim, and the GPT-series experiments (A.9.2) showing strong intrinsic self-awareness without training are a valuable finding.
Reproducibility is good: models, datasets, hyperparameters, and prompts are documented in detail, and the routing overhead (<5%) is empirically justified rather than simply assumed away.
weaknesses: Novelty over prior work is moderate. The core mechanism—cascade ordered by cost with per-model abstention—is closely related to FrugalGPT and early-abstention cascades, and AgentNet shares the decentralized motivation. The main new elements are the framing and the scenario-conditioned local reward; the authors should sharpen the delta relative to these baselines.

The main experiments use a homogeneous model pool (five sizes of one family, Qwen2.5). Heterogeneous-pool validation is relegated to the appendix and only partially substitutes for a same-family pool, which is the most common industrial setting.

Costs are synthetic, fixed, normalized values rather than real monetary or latency-adjusted costs measured per scenario; while latency is analyzed separately, the utility metric conflates heterogeneous cost definitions across the main and appendix setups (GPU time in A.3 vs. API pricing in A.9.2).

The external-router comparison in Table 5 (the crux of the 'intrinsic beats external' claim) uses a RoBERTa-base classifier and a Llama3-8B classifier, both weaker than what a well-tuned external router could be; the claim 'intrinsic assessment is more effective' is somewhat overgeneralized from this comparison.

Some inconsistencies and sloppiness: indexing error in Equation 1 (sum from i=0), minor grammar issues ('To further enhancing', 'prevent itself from queries'), and results such as DiSRouter underperforming baselines on some OOD scenarios (Table 13, SFT variant) are glossed over in the narrative, which emphasizes only the +RL results.

Scalability of the training pipeline is a concern: self-awareness training requires per-model SFT+RL, and the paper does not quantify the compute cost of adding a new agent versus retraining a centralized router, weakening the practical scalability argument.
